questions.stem: An off-duty nurse stops to help at a car crash and gives first aid. What protects the nurse legally?

options.text: Good Samaritan laws, as long as the nurse acts within training and without gross negligence
The hospital's malpractice insurance
Nothing; nurses should never help off duty
The client's signed consent

rationale.correct: Good Samaritan laws protect good-faith emergency care within the person's training.

perOption.a: These laws protect people who give emergency help in good faith without payment.
perOption.b: Usually covers only work done for the employer.
perOption.c: Helping in good faith is encouraged and protected.
perOption.d: Consent isn't practical in an emergency.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which situations must the nurse report to the proper authorities as required by law in most states? Select all that apply.

options.text: A gunshot wound
Suspected abuse of a dependent adult
A new diagnosis of measles
A client's seasonal allergy
A client's decision to refuse surgery
A positive syphilis test

rationale.correct: Mandatory reports include certain injuries, abuse and communicable diseases.

perOption.a: Most states require reporting gunshot and stab wounds.
perOption.b: Nurses are mandated reporters of elder and dependent adult abuse.
perOption.c: Measles is a reportable communicable disease.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a confused client, "If you try to get up again, I'll tie you to the bed." Which tort does this describe?

options.text: Assault
Battery
Defamation
Invasion of privacy

rationale.correct: Assault is a threat; battery is unwanted touching.

perOption.a: Assault is a threat that makes a person fear harmful contact.
perOption.b: Battery is actual touching without consent.
perOption.c: Defamation is a false statement that harms someone's reputation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A competent client who is admitted voluntarily is kept from leaving the unit by staff locking the door. Which tort does this describe?

options.text: False imprisonment
Negligence
Libel
Abandonment

rationale.correct: Competent clients may leave unless a lawful hold applies.

perOption.a: Unlawfully restricting a competent person's movement is false imprisonment.
perOption.b: Negligence is failure to meet the standard of care.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which document defines the legal scope of practice for registered nurses in a state?

options.text: The state's nurse practice act
The hospital's policy manual
The ANA Code of Ethics
The client bill of rights

rationale.correct: The nurse practice act sets the legal scope of nursing practice.

perOption.a: Each state's nurse practice act defines scope of practice and licensure.
perOption.b: Policies can't expand legal scope.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the source of scope of practice.

questions.stem: A nurse sees a post on social media by a coworker that includes a photo of a client's wound with no face shown. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore it because the client can't be identified
Report it according to facility policy
Like the post to show support
Share the post with other nurses for learning

rationale.correct: Never post client information or images on social media.

perOption.a: Details can still identify a client, and posting violates policy and privacy.
perOption.b: Posting client images without consent violates privacy and professional standards.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a social media privacy breach.

questions.stem: Which situation shows all four elements of malpractice (duty, breach, causation, harm)?

options.text: A nurse forgets to document a vital sign that was normal
A nurse doesn't report a client's falling blood pressure, and the client later has a stroke from untreated hemorrhage
A client falls despite every fall precaution being in place
A nurse gives a medication late, and the client has no effects

rationale.correct: Malpractice requires duty, breach, causation and damages.

perOption.a: No harm resulted.
perOption.b: Duty existed, the standard was breached, and the breach caused harm.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client arrives at the emergency department in active labor but has no insurance. What is the legal requirement?

options.text: Transfer the client to a public hospital immediately
Provide a medical screening exam and stabilizing treatment regardless of ability to pay
Ask for payment before treatment
Refuse care because of the hospital's policy

rationale.correct: EMTALA requires emergency screening and stabilization regardless of payment.

perOption.a: Transfer before stabilization violates EMTALA.
perOption.b: EMTALA requires screening and stabilization for anyone who comes to the ED.
perOption.c: Not allowed before screening and stabilization.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each situation, indicate the ethical principle that is most at stake.

rows.text: A competent client refuses dialysis after being told the risks
Deciding which of two clients gets the last ICU bed
Holding a sedative that would further lower a client's dangerously low blood pressure
Spending extra time helping a frightened client understand the plan

rationale.correct: Autonomy is self-determination, beneficence is doing good, justice is fairness, and nonmaleficence is avoiding harm.

perOption.r3:c2: Related, but the focus is avoiding harm.
perOption.r4:c1: Related, but the focus is doing good.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client dying of cancer receives increasing doses of morphine for severe pain. The family worries the morphine may shorten life. Which principle supports giving it?

options.text: The principle of double effect
Paternalism
Fidelity
Veracity

rationale.correct: Double effect: the intent is pain relief, not hastening death.

perOption.a: An action intended to relieve suffering is ethical even if a foreseen but unintended effect occurs.
perOption.b: Overriding a client's wishes; not relevant here.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain the principle of double effect.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to take part in a procedure that conflicts with the nurse's personal beliefs. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Refuse in front of the client
Tell the supervisor ahead of time and make sure the client's care is handed off safely
Leave the unit without telling anyone
Try to talk the client out of the procedure

rationale.correct: Conscientious objection requires notice and safe transfer of care.

perOption.a: Unprofessional and distressing to the client.
perOption.b: Conscientious objection is acceptable when care isn't abandoned.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who is deaf and uses American Sign Language needs teaching before a procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Write notes in English
Arrange a qualified ASL interpreter
Ask a family member to sign
Speak slowly and loudly

rationale.correct: Use qualified sign language interpreters.

perOption.a: ASL users may not read English fluently.
perOption.b: Clients are entitled to effective communication.
perOption.c: Family interpreters may be inaccurate and breach privacy.
perOption.d: Not effective for a deaf client.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client says, "The doctor said the surgery is my only option, but I wanted to hear about others." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client the doctor knows best
Tell the provider the client wants to discuss alternatives before consenting
Explain alternatives in detail to the client
Cancel the surgery

rationale.correct: Nurses advocate by making sure clients get the information they need.

perOption.a: Doesn't respect the client's right to information.
perOption.b: Advocacy supports informed decision-making.
perOption.c: The provider explains the options as part of informed consent.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old asks to be tested and treated for a sexually transmitted infection without telling the parents. What applies in most states?

options.text: The minor can consent to STI testing and treatment
Parental consent is always required
The nurse must call the parents
Testing must wait until age 18

rationale.correct: Minors can consent to some services, such as STI care, contraception and substance use treatment, depending on state law.

perOption.a: Most states let minors consent to STI care.
perOption.b: STI care is a common exception.

questions.stem: A client is asked to join a research study. Which statement by the client shows understanding of research consent?

options.text: "I have to stay in the study once I sign."
"I can leave the study at any time without losing my usual care."
"My care will be worse if I don't join."
"The researchers don't need to tell me the risks."

rationale.correct: Research consent is voluntary, informed and can be withdrawn.

perOption.a: Participants can withdraw at any time.
perOption.b: Voluntary participation and withdrawal are required.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a valid POLST form stating "comfort measures only" stops breathing. The family asks staff to start CPR. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Start CPR because the family asked
Follow the POLST, notify the provider and support the family
Call the hospital lawyer before doing anything
Ask the family to sign a new form

rationale.correct: Honor valid advance directives and POLST orders.

perOption.a: The client's documented wishes take priority.
perOption.b: A POLST is a medical order reflecting the client's wishes.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: Two adult children of an unconscious client disagree about continuing life support. The client has no advance directive. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the wishes of the oldest child
Request an ethics consultation and a family meeting with the team
Stop life support
Take a vote among all family members

rationale.correct: Ethics committees help resolve surrogate disagreements.

perOption.a: Age isn't the basis for surrogate decisions.
perOption.b: Ethics consultation helps resolve conflicts about care.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A nurse wants to look up a neighbor's lab results because the neighbor is a client in the hospital. What is correct?

options.text: It's fine because the nurse has system access
Access only records needed for your assigned work
It's fine if the neighbor wouldn't mind
It's fine if the nurse doesn't tell anyone

rationale.correct: Access client records only as needed for your role.

perOption.a: Access is only for clients the nurse is caring for.
perOption.b: HIPAA's minimum necessary standard limits access to job duties.
perOption.d: Unauthorized access is still a violation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

Use the facility's downtime procedures and paper forms
Write notes on scrap paper and throw them away later
Tell clients to come back later

rationale.correct: Know the facility's downtime procedures.

perOption.a: Care continues using downtime procedures.
perOption.b: Downtime procedures keep care and documentation safe.

questions.stem: Which documentation practice in the electronic health record is unsafe?

options.text: Copying the previous shift's assessment forward without reassessing
Documenting soon after care
Logging off when leaving the computer
Documenting a client's refusal of care

rationale.correct: Document only what you assessed; avoid copy-and-paste errors.

perOption.a: Copy-forward can record findings that are no longer true.
perOption.b: Timely documentation is correct.

options.text: Override the alert because alerts are frequent
Read the alert and check with the pharmacist or provider before giving the drug
Give half the dose
Turn off alerts for the unit

rationale.correct: Respond to clinical decision support alerts thoughtfully.

perOption.a: Alert fatigue causes errors.
perOption.b: Alerts may show real risks.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving a handoff using I-PASS. Place the parts in order.

items.text: Action list: what must be done and by when
Patient summary: diagnosis, events and plan
Synthesis by receiver: the receiving nurse summarizes

rationale.correct: I-PASS: Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness, Synthesis.

perOption.a: Tells the receiver how worried to be.
perOption.b: Gives context.
perOption.d: What could go wrong and what to do.

questions.stem: During a code, the team leader asks the nurse to give epinephrine 1 mg IV. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it without speaking to save time
Repeat the order back, give it and announce when it's given
Wait for a written order
Ask another nurse to decide

rationale.correct: Closed-loop communication: repeat back, carry out, confirm.

perOption.a: Closed-loop communication prevents errors.
perOption.b: Closed-loop communication confirms each order.
perOption.c: Verbal orders are used in emergencies.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: The nurse reviews a colleague's documentation. Highlight the entries that are inappropriate.

segments.text: Client resting quietly, respirations 16, SpO2 96% on room air.
Client is being difficult and lazy about walking.
Client found sitting on the floor beside the bed; denies pain; provider notified at 10:07.
Dr. Lee made an error with the order again.

rationale.correct: Document facts objectively; leave out opinions, blame and references to incident reports.

perOption.s6: Incident reports aren't mentioned in the medical record.
perOption.s10: Blaming statements don't belong in the record.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: Which actions support a client with low health literacy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use plain language and avoid medical jargon
Use the teach-back method
Give large amounts of written information at once
Focus on the two or three most important points
Use pictures or demonstrations
Ask "Do you understand?" and move on

rationale.correct: Health literacy strategies: plain language, teach-back, few key points, visuals.

perOption.a: Improves understanding.
perOption.b: Confirms understanding.
perOption.f: Clients may say yes without understanding.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A nurse with a multistate license lives in one compact state and wants to work in another compact state. What is true?

options.text: The nurse must get a new license in the second state
The nurse may practice in other compact states under the home-state multistate license
The nurse can practice anywhere in the world
The nurse must give up the home-state license

rationale.correct: The Nurse Licensure Compact lets nurses practice across member states.

perOption.a: The compact allows practice in other member states.
perOption.b: The Nurse Licensure Compact allows this, following each state's practice laws.
perOption.c: The compact covers member states only.

questions.stem: A nurse reports repeated unsafe staffing to the manager with no change. The nurse is now considering reporting to an outside agency. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Nurses who report unsafe conditions in good faith are often protected by whistleblower laws
Nurses can be fired for any outside report
Nurses should post the issue on social media
Nurses must stay silent to protect the facility

rationale.correct: Use internal channels first; whistleblower protections support good-faith reporting.

perOption.a: Many laws protect good-faith reporting.
perOption.b: Whistleblower protections exist in many states.
